cues.text: One Will or Two? The Monothelite Compromise
By the seventh century, the Church had lived for two hundred years with the painful Monophysite schism that followed Chalcedon's declaration of Christ's two natures.
Seeking a formula that might win the Monophysites back without repudiating Chalcedon, some churchmen proposed a middle path.
Whatever the number of Christ's natures , perhaps he had only one will and one energy (operation) , a divine-human will acting as a single principle.
This position came to be called Monothelitism ("one-will-ism").

The Patriarch of Constantinople, Sergius , promoted the idea with the backing of Emperor Heraclius , whose empire faced Persian and then Arab invasions and badly needed the political unity reconciliation might bring.
Even Pope Honorius I was drawn into apparent sympathy with the formula in a private letter, a fact that would trouble his memory for centuries afterward.
But the monk St. Maximus the Confessor and, eventually, Pope St. Martin I recognized Monothelitism as a subtle denial of Christ's full and active humanity.
For a nature without its own will, they argued, is no real nature at all.
Persecution and a Roman Council
Opposition came at a steep price.
Emperor Constans II issued the Typus in 648, forbidding all further discussion of one or two wills in Christ under penalty of law.
Pope Martin I defied the edict by convening the Lateran Council of 649 , which condemned Monothelitism outright.
In retaliation, Byzantine agents seized Martin, dragged him to Constantinople, and exiled him to the Crimea.
There, he died from the harsh treatment.
Maximus the Confessor was likewise arrested, tortured — his tongue and right hand were mutilated to silence his preaching and writing — and exiled, dying shortly after in 662.
The political climate shifted with the accession of Constantine IV in 668, a far more conciliatory emperor who sought to heal the breach with Rome rather than enforce Monothelitism by force.
The Council in the Domed Hall

Constantine IV summoned bishops to Constantinople in 680, and the council opened on November 7, 680 in a domed hall of the imperial palace, the trullus , meeting under his personal presidency for its first eleven sessions.
Legates of Pope St. Agatho brought a lengthy dogmatic letter setting out the orthodox position; attendance grew over the eighteen sessions from around 100 bishops to a final 174 signatories.

George , the Patriarch of Constantinople, accepted the orthodox teaching of two wills and operations early in the proceedings, but Macarius of Antioch held out to the end as Monothelitism's last determined defender and was deposed and anathematized.

In a startling and historically consequential move, the council also examined the private correspondence of the earlier Pope Honorius I. Finding his letters compatible with Monothelite language, it anathematized him by name alongside the other Monothelite leaders—a judgment later popes accepted, understanding Honorius to have erred through ambiguity and negligence rather than through a formal, binding definition of faith.
Two Wills, Two Operations
The council's definition, issued in its final session on September 16, 681 , declared that Christ possesses two natural wills and two natural operations , divine and human.
It described them as existing "without division, without change, without separation, without confusion" — deliberately echoing Chalcedon's language two centuries earlier.
His human will, the council taught, is not opposed to his divine will but follows it in perfect, willing obedience, "not as if overpowered or forced, but as following."

The council anathematized Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Honorius as promoters of the heresy, formally closing the Monothelite chapter of the Christological controversies that had run continuously from Nestorius through Chalcedon to this point.
Legacy
The Sixth Ecumenical Council completed the Christological definitions begun at Nicaea in 325.
It filled out the Church's teaching that Christ, one Person in two natures, likewise acts through two complete and unconfused wills.
This fully affirmed the reality and integrity of his human nature down to its very freedom to choose.
Monothelitism briefly revived under Emperor Philippicus Bardanes in the early eighth century, but never regained serious traction after 681.
The council's condemnation of Pope Honorius became, centuries later, a point of careful study during debates over papal infallibility.
It demonstrated that a pope's private letters and personal theological opinions carry a different weight than a solemn, formal definition of faith addressed to the whole Church.
